claims.claim: Schaeffer and colleagues' twelve one-sided paired t-tests on the min-p paper's data supported min-p's superiority in one of twelve comparisons after Bonferroni correction at alpha 0.05.
claims.source: Rylan Schaeffer, Joshua Kazdan and Yegor Denisov-Blanch (Stanford University), 'Min-p, Max Exaggeration: A Critical Analysis of Min-p Sampling in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 19 Jun 2025

claims.claim: Schaeffer and colleagues, annotating the min-p study's free-text responses, found that more human evaluators explicitly preferred plain temperature sampling than preferred min-p.
claims.source: Rylan Schaeffer, Joshua Kazdan and Yegor Denisov-Blanch (Stanford University), 'Min-p, Max Exaggeration: A Critical Analysis of Min-p Sampling in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 19 Jun 2025
claims.quote: more human evaluators explicitly preferred basic sampling than preferred min-p

claims.claim: Schaeffer and colleagues report that the min-p paper's creative-writing table gave the higher of two available scores for min-p and the lower of two for top-p.
claims.source: Rylan Schaeffer, Joshua Kazdan and Yegor Denisov-Blanch (Stanford University), 'Min-p, Max Exaggeration: A Critical Analysis of Min-p Sampling in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 19 Jun 2025
claims.quote: the higher of two scores was reported for min-p

claims.claim: Schaeffer and colleagues conclude that all the samplers they swept perform roughly the same once each is given the same amount of hyperparameter tuning.
claims.source: Rylan Schaeffer, Joshua Kazdan and Yegor Denisov-Blanch (Stanford University), 'Min-p, Max Exaggeration: A Critical Analysis of Min-p Sampling in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 19 Jun 2025
claims.quote: all samplers perform roughly the same once given the same
claims.page: section 6, Discussion and Limitations, Scientific Conclusions

claims.claim: Schaeffer and colleagues allow that min-p may sometimes help at higher temperatures, with the caveat that absolute performance in that regime is meaningfully worse than at standard temperatures.
claims.source: Rylan Schaeffer, Joshua Kazdan and Yegor Denisov-Blanch (Stanford University), 'Min-p, Max Exaggeration: A Critical Analysis of Min-p Sampling in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 19 Jun 2025
claims.quote: min-p sampling can sometimes provide a benefit at higher temperatures

claims.claim: Paech and colleagues measured that some over-used patterns appear over one thousand times more often in language-model output than in human text.
claims.source: Samuel J Paech, Allen G Roush, Judah Goldfeder and Ravid Shwartz-Ziv, 'Antislop: A Comprehensive Framework for Identifying and Eliminating Repetitive Patterns in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 21 Oct 2025
claims.quote: slop patterns appear over 1,000× more frequently in LLM output

claims.claim: Paech and colleagues measured that the name Elara appears 85,513 times more often in gemma-3-12b's creative writing than in their human baseline.
claims.source: Samuel J Paech, Allen G Roush, Judah Goldfeder and Ravid Shwartz-Ziv, 'Antislop: A Comprehensive Framework for Identifying and Eliminating Repetitive Patterns in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 21 Oct 2025
claims.page: section 3.2, Empirical Findings, discussion of Table 1

claims.claim: Paech and colleagues found the trigram 'voice barely whisper' among the top forty over-represented trigrams of 68.7 percent of the sixty-seven models they profiled.
claims.source: Samuel J Paech, Allen G Roush, Judah Goldfeder and Ravid Shwartz-Ziv, 'Antislop: A Comprehensive Framework for Identifying and Eliminating Repetitive Patterns in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 21 Oct 2025
claims.page: Table 5 (Top overlapping trigrams across 67 AI models)

claims.claim: Paech and colleagues state that stochastic decoding strategies such as top-k, top-p and min-p do not address a model's repetitive tendencies in outputs that are already coherent.
claims.source: Samuel J Paech, Allen G Roush, Judah Goldfeder and Ravid Shwartz-Ziv, 'Antislop: A Comprehensive Framework for Identifying and Eliminating Repetitive Patterns in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 21 Oct 2025
claims.quote: these strategies do not address repetitive tendencies in coherent outputs

claims.claim: Paech and colleagues measured that their backtracking Antislop sampler suppressed banned patterns completely while scoring above the baseline model on their writing-quality rubric.
claims.source: Samuel J Paech, Allen G Roush, Judah Goldfeder and Ravid Shwartz-Ziv, 'Antislop: A Comprehensive Framework for Identifying and Eliminating Repetitive Patterns in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 21 Oct 2025
claims.quote: The Antislop Sampler achieves perfect suppression (100%)

claims.claim: Paech and colleagues measured that plain token banning at eight thousand patterns dropped writing quality to 28 out of 100 on their rubric.
claims.source: Samuel J Paech, Allen G Roush, Judah Goldfeder and Ravid Shwartz-Ziv, 'Antislop: A Comprehensive Framework for Identifying and Eliminating Repetitive Patterns in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 21 Oct 2025
claims.quote: quality falling to 28 (out of 100) at 8k patterns

claims.claim: Paech and colleagues measured that DPO fine-tuning on their slop preference pairs collapsed lexical diversity to between 74 and 92 percent of the baseline model's.
claims.source: Samuel J Paech, Allen G Roush, Judah Goldfeder and Ravid Shwartz-Ziv, 'Antislop: A Comprehensive Framework for Identifying and Eliminating Repetitive Patterns in Language Models', arXiv preprint v2, 21 Oct 2025

claims.claim: Paech explains that per-token logit biasing cannot suppress most over-used phrases because they span more than one token, which is why his sampler waits for the whole phrase and backtracks.
claims.source: Sam Paech, antislop-sampler README (GitHub), updated 13 Oct 2024
claims.quote: most slop words & phrases are more than one token

claims.claim: Paech states that his default slop list was computed as words over-represented in language-model output relative to normal human writing.
claims.source: Sam Paech, antislop-sampler README (GitHub), updated 13 Oct 2024
claims.quote: over-represented in LLM output compared to normal human writing

claims.claim: Paech states that his Slop Score looks for glaringly over-used patterns rather than classifying a text as machine or human, and will not reliably help a writer evade AI detectors.
claims.source: Sam Paech, 'Slop Score' explainer page, EQ-Bench (eqbench.com), read 6 Sep 2026
claims.quote: It looks for glaringly over-used patterns, rather than trying to classify
claims.page: 'How does this work?' panel, 'Not an AI Detector!'

verdicts.trueWording: min-p's superiority in 1 of 12 comparisons at alpha=0.05
verdicts.note: arXiv HTML v2 fetched raw (200). Table 1 caption states exactly this after Bonferroni; Sec 2.3 confirms '12 one-sided paired t-tests' run 'using the authors' published data' (df=52, alternative=greater). Graded SUBSTANCE not VERBATIM only because the claim ships an empty quote field.

verdicts.trueWording: more human evaluators explicitly preferred basic sampling than preferred min-p
verdicts.note: Sec 2.3, result (1), word for word (page continues 'sampling'). Annotation limb supported: 'We manually annotated responses from human annotators regarding their preferred sampler(s)', free-text answers quoted in Appendix A. 'Plain temperature sampling' is a fair gloss of the paper's 'basic' sampler, defined in Sec 1 as temperature-only and in Sec 3.1 as having 'only a temperature hyperparameter'.

verdicts.trueWording: the higher of two scores was reported for min-p
verdicts.note: Sec 4.3 body, word for word; the section heading states the same for Table 3(b), and the sentence continues that the lower of two was reported for top-p (52.01 vs 50.14 for min-p; 50.07 vs 50.43 for top-p). Creative-writing limb supported: Sec 4 introduces these as the original paper's 'AlpacaEval creative writing evaluations'.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that Schaeffer and colleagues 'conclude' this flatly - the page hedges the same sentence, saying the data 'suggest' it and that 'more research would be needed to assess the veracity of this conclusion'
verdicts.trueWording: all samplers perform roughly the same once given the same
verdicts.note: Quote is verbatim in Sec 6, Scientific Conclusions. Full sentence: the original paper's data and their extensions 'suggest' this, 'however, in our view, more research would be needed to assess the veracity of this conclusion'. The samplers-swept limb is fine (Sec 3.1 sweeps four: basic, top-p, top-k, min-p). Downgraded because the claim drops the authors' own explicit hedge and reports a suggestion as a settled conclusion.

verdicts.trueWording: min-p sampling can sometimes provide a benefit at higher temperatures
verdicts.note: Sec 6, Discussion and Limitations, word for word. The caveat limb is the same sentence: 'albeit with the critical caveat that absolute performance is meaningfully worse in this high-temperature regime than in standard temperature regimes'. The page's lead-in is 'The paper's data does weakly suggest', which matches the claim's hedged 'allow that... may sometimes'.

verdicts.trueWording: some slop patterns appear over 1,000x more frequently in LLM output
verdicts.note: Abstract, word for word (page renders the multiplication sign; sentence ends 'than human text'). Sec 1 repeats it as 'some patterns occur over 1000x more frequently in LLM text than in human writing'. arXiv HTML v2 fetched raw (200).

verdicts.trueWording: Elara appears 85,513 times more frequently in gemma-3-12b's creative writing
verdicts.note: Sec 3.2 text under Table 1, word for word; page says 'than in human text', and the Table 1 caption defines that baseline as 'wordfreq + Reddit/Gutenberg corpora' over 2,000 gemma-3-12b creative-writing samples. Table 1's own row for 'elara' reads 85,513x.

verdicts.trueWording: 'voice barely whisper' appearing on 68.7% of lists
verdicts.note: Appendix G text gives the figure; Table 5's row for 'voice barely whisper' is 68.7 and its caption reads 'Top overlapping trigrams across 67 AI models... % of models in which the phrase appears among their top 40 most over-represented trigrams'. Every limb (top forty, 68.7 percent, sixty-seven models) checks out. Graded SUBSTANCE only because the claim ships an empty quote field.

verdicts.trueWording: these strategies do not address repetitive tendencies in coherent outputs
verdicts.note: Sec 2, Related Work, word for word (preceded by 'However,'). The antecedent is the prior sentence: 'Stochastic decoding strategies like top-k, top-p (nucleus sampling), and min-p... have since been adopted to increase diversity and reduce incoherent outputs', so the named-samplers limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: Antislop Sampler achieves perfect suppression (100%) while actually improving writing quality
verdicts.note: Sec 6.2, Main Results, word for word; the sentence ends 'above baseline', and the preceding sentence names the axis as 'output degradation as measured by our writing rubric'. Backtracking limb supported by the Abstract: the sampler 'uses backtracking to suppress unwanted strings at inference time'.

verdicts.trueWording: quality falling to 28 (out of 100) at 8k patterns
verdicts.note: Sec 6.2, Main Results, word for word, in the sentence 'Token banning collapses even more severely, with quality falling to 28 (out of 100) at 8k patterns'. Rubric limb supported by the same subsection's writing-rubric metric definition; 'plain token banning' is the paper's 'token banning' baseline.

CITATION MISMATCH, flagged: the supplied quote 'FTPO maintains or enhances diversity' is on the page word for word but describes FTPO (95-102% of baseline), not the DPO collapse the claim asserts. The claim's own substance is fully supported by the second half of that Sec 6.3 sentence, 'while DPO causes progressive collapse (74-92%)', diversity being normalized to the baseline model at 100. Do not carry the supplied quote as the citation for this claim; the DPO run is trained on their final-token preference set.

verdicts.trueWording: most slop words & phrases are more than one token
verdicts.note: README section 'What this does:', word for word, in 'Previous approaches have done this with per-token logit biasing; but that's quite ineffective since most slop words & phrases are more than one token'. Backtracking limb is the next sentence ('we wait for the whole phrase to appear... then backtrack'). The strong 'cannot suppress' reading is carried by the later 'Samplers typically work at the token level -- but that doesn't work if [you] want to avoid words/phrases that tokenise to >1 tokens'; the nearer wording is the softer 'quite ineffective'.

verdicts.trueWording: over-represented in LLM output compared to normal human writing
verdicts.note: README section 'What this does:', word for word: 'For the default slop list, we computed a large list of words that are over-represented in LLM output compared to normal human writing.' Completeness note for downstream use (not a failed limb, since the claim asserts derivation and not exclusivity): the same sentence adds that the list 'is supplemented by a list of over-used phrases that are pet peeves of LLM enthusiasts', and the README elsewhere calls the shipped JSON 'mostly auto-generated' and 'not well optimised or curated'.

verdicts.trueWording: It looks for glaringly over-used patterns, rather than trying to classify
verdicts.note: Live page fetched raw (200), 'How does this work?' panel, 'Not an AI Detector!' subsection, word for word; sentence continues 'the text as AI or human'. Second limb is the next sentence: 'it won't reliably help you avoid AI detection'. Attribution to Paech rests on the panel's source link to github.com/sam-paech/slop-score and the EQ-Bench host, not on a byline in the page text.
